title.official: Punishment for civil contempt of Court

operative_text.controlling:
10.53(1)  Every person declared to be in civil contempt of Court is
liable to any one or more of the following penalties or sanctions in
the discretion of a judge:
(a) imprisonment until the person has purged the person’s
contempt;
(b) imprisonment for not more than 2 years;
(c) a fine and, in default of paying the fine, imprisonment for
not more than 6 months;
(d) if the person is a party to an action, application or
proceeding, an order that
(i) all or part of a commencement document, affidavit or
pleading be struck out,
(ii) an action or an application be stayed,
(iii) a claim, action, defence, application or proceeding be
dismissed, or judgment be entered or an order be
made, or
(iv) a record or evidence be prohibited from being used
or entered in an application, proceeding or at trial.
(2)  The Court may also make a costs award against a person
declared to be in civil contempt of Court.
(3)  If a person declared to be in civil contempt of Court purges the
person’s contempt, the Court may waive or suspend any penalty or
sanction.
(4)  The judge who imposed a penalty or sanction for civil
contempt may, on notice to the person concerned, increase, vary or
remit the penalty or sanction.

BOOK_A.commentary:
pleading, record
A. Introduction
Generally on penalties for contempt, see the discussion and authorities in the textbooks.¹
The penalty for contempt is not limited to what is listed in R.10.53. The Court may substitute
a more comprehensive simpler ban harder to argue about.²
Contempt is intended both to punish and to end the wrong conduct.³
And to deter such
misconduct by others.⁴
One must remember that contempt is not the only way to enforce a court order. In many
cases the Civil Enforcement Act will offer a variety of remedies, either instead or in addition. And
if someone fails to convey property as ordered, the court may authorize a court ofﬁcial to sign the
conveyance.⁵
See further R.10.52 n. M.
On whether part of R.10.53 is unconstitutional, see the reference to litigation in the Turkawski
case.⁶
B. Penalties
1. Aims and Aggravation
A number of criteria for sentencing and weight of penalty are reviewed.⁷
Continuing earlier
deliberate deﬁance, with little attempt to purge the contempt, and stubbornness, and refusal to
pay any costs, were bad⁸
and led to striking out the contemnor's pleadings.⁹
Furthermore, both the common law and Rr.10.53(1) (a), 10.53(3) and 10.53(4) allow the
court to suspend, end, vary, or remit a penalty for contempt.¹⁰
That can be done to encourage
belated obedience by the contemnor and encourage his or her undoing the effects of his or
her contempt.¹¹
Or it can be done retroactively to give him or her credit for such restitution or

repentance.¹
Encouraging compliance (rather than punishing) is important where the contempt
was failure to give discovery.²
If there is no public deﬁance, contempt is usually more a matter of enforcement than of
punishment, though orders often properly seek to do both.³
If a penalty is imposed for a continuing
disobedience, it is useful for the court to indicate how much of that penalty is for the past and so
irrevocable, and how much is for the future and so might be reduced or discharged if there is later
obedience.⁴
But continued deliberate and dishonest disobedience produces a need for a penalty
to deter the miscreant and others tempted to do the same.⁵
Aggravating circumstances for a higher penalty include being a lawyer, the potential beneﬁts
(savings) of disobedience, public nature of the contempt, the harm done to the opposing party
(including thrown-away costs) and to the court (though compensation is not a licensing fee or
substitute for the penalty), the motive for disobeying, other consequences, the context, the degree
of culpability of each person, the nature of the contempt, whether the disobedience was reported,
knowledge and understanding, displays of deﬁance, effects on the public, need for deterrence,
and ability to pay.⁶
That a party (eventually and reluctantly) purged his contempt and ﬁnally obeyed an order, is
no reason to decline to decide whether he had been in contempt before that. Purging is relevant
only to the size of the penalty.⁷
A continuing failure to obey a mandatory order (e. g. to produce items) is not a continuing
contempt allowing repeated convictions, nor allowing additions to an existing ﬁxed-length jail
sentence. A new conviction requires a new actus reus. But if the injunction is negative, a new act
is a new actus reus.⁸
An indeﬁnite sentence until the contempt is purged may be appropriate.⁹
And breach of more court orders after the contempt conviction is relevant too.¹⁰

2. Jail¹
It was sometimes suggested that jail is not imposed in Alberta for contempt, but that is not
correct. Most such sentences are merely not in writing or reported; some have no recorded
reasons, especially as the reasons are oral.²
A few days’ jail for breach of a restraining order is
common, and in many cases time in custody is imposed after someone has been arrested while
breaching an order.³
Ninety days in jail plus community service, was imposed on a disbarred
lawyer who very persistently for years kept practising law despite court orders forbidding that.⁴
Even indeterminate jail sentences are known, and the only limit is 5 years (because there is a
right to a jury over 5 years).⁵
There is full power to order community service as a penalty, and it need not be structured as
a condition (e. g. for remission of jail).⁶
The court has inherent power to impose other remedies or punishments not listed in the Rules
of Court for contempt, so long as they meet judicial criteria.⁷
3. Fines
Fines are important penalties for contempt of court, though ability to pay and surrounding
circumstances must be carefully looked at; some case law reviewed.⁸
Financial penalties under R.10.49(1) and R.10.53(1) (c) are to be paid to the Government of
Alberta, not to individual litigants.⁹
There is no longer any ceiling on the ﬁne which may be imposed.¹⁰
$400, 000 was upheld for
two public contempts in the United Nurses case.¹¹
$400, 000 ﬁne for a single instance of civil
contempt was too high. Its publicity and the intent are not relevant if the conviction is for civil, not

criminal, contempt. The ﬁne was cut to $200, 000.¹
For wrongly gaining revenues of $6 million, the
contemnor paid a $500, 000 ﬁne plus full indemnity costs, plus $29, 000 paid under a settlement to
be repaid.²
Breach of an Alberta injunction against pursuing proceedings abroad led to a further
Alberta order to abandon both those proceedings, on threat of $1 million ﬁne (plus $10, 000 a
day).³
Flagrant and repeated disobedience of a court order (by self-represented parties), here led
to a $1000 ﬁne (payable to the Clerk), plus full-indemnity costs. In default of payment of either,
the upcoming summary judgment motion by the parties would be stayed and not re-scheduled
without such payments (despite long waits to get that scheduled date).⁴
For continuing long-standing failure to obey a court order to produce certain records, a ﬁne of
$1, 500 was imposed, plus $100 extra for each future calendar day until full compliance.⁵
It was proper to use a large ﬁne paid for contempt of court in a civil matter, to pay the
psychologists involved in treating the children, but the father paying the ﬁne was not to be
considered to have paid for that counselling. He paid the court as punishment.⁶
Even with continued contempt (disobeying court orders), another judge cannot vary a contempt
penalty set by the ﬁrst judge.⁷
4. Procedural Penalties
See also Part D below.
Pleadings are often struck out,⁸
or an action is commonly stayed,⁹
to enforce compliance, but
it is not often proceeded with once compliance has been secured.¹⁰
But if default goes on long
enough and after enough orders or warnings, pleadings may be struck out. That is because the

courts and the public are less willing to waste scarce resources on the contumelious or extremely
lax litigant; most litigation is too slow as it is.¹
Where a litigant persists in disobeying an order for
better discovery, the Court may strike out his pleading if he does not comply.²
His own discovery
may be ended.³
For the plaintiff's repeated disobedience of orders to renew letters of credit given as security,
the suit would be dismissed, unless within 5 days the security was restored.⁴
Persistent contempt
and failure to purge it, led to a penalty of dismissing the contemnor's pending application to add a
new defendant to existing litigation.⁵
The remedy of forbidding a party to adduce certain evidence⁶
is a good one which is not used
enough.⁷
A party who ﬂees and adduces no evidence risks losing even a child custody ﬁght: not
as a penalty, but because only the other side’s evidence is available.⁸
Persistent contempt can produce other enforcement measures outside the litigation, such as
vacating premises while a realtor is there to inspect or show property which the court has ordered
sold.⁹
If the contemnor is an executor or trustee, all compensation from the estate for services or
expenses may be denied him or her.¹⁰
C. Costs
If contempt is found, costs should be imposed (on top of any penalty). Usually full indemnity
is the appropriate level. Those costs are not just a sanction or a declaration; the innocent party
should not have to pay for the publicly-vital task of enforcing court orders. Otherwise the innocent
party is being punished.¹¹

Conviction for contempt usually leads to heavy costs as well as any penalty.¹
The costs are
remedial. Partial indemnity thrown-away party-party costs are not a sufﬁcient remedy for deliberate
breach of a court order. A substantial portion of the expenses directly caused should ordinarily
be a minimum.²
Often “solicitor-client” (full indemnity) costs are ordered.³
In one case,⁴
the hourly
rate of the lawyer applying was low, so slightly enhanced solicitor-client costs were upheld on
appeal.⁵
In another case the contemnor paid $136, 000 costs (plus a hefty ﬁne).⁶
The penalty will
be inﬂuenced by the role of counsel, motives, consequences of the acts, the history of the suit,
expense caused to others, and degree of culpability.⁷
A protestor in contempt of an injunction
though he thought he had a right to protest, may have to pay a proportionate share of the costs.⁸
A defendant found guilty of contempt partway through the suit had to pay costs at once, not
at the end of the suit, to impose discipline on the litigation process, given the nature of contempt,
because an earlier order had set dates to pay the costs. Costs are paid forthwith, and there were
no special circumstances.⁹
Contempt was found and not purged, but trial would come in a few months and the steps about
contempt and about getting to trial could not be easily separated, so the trial judge should deal
with all the costs, even those for contempt.¹⁰
Costs imposed by a justice as a penalty for contempt cannot ordinarily be reversed by another
justice later.¹¹
D. Party in Contempt Cannot Make Application
Contempt of court does more than expose the guilty person to the penalties for contempt set
out in R.10.53. It also bars that person from taking any active voluntary positive step in court
while he or she is still in contempt.¹²
The contempt does not bar self-defence, but it does bar

appeals from anything but the contempt ﬁnding.¹
An appeal over custody may be adjourned until
the appellant purges her contempt by bringing the children back to Alberta.²
An act contrary to an
order may be void for illegality.³
Here the ﬁne levied for the contempts found had been paid. The costs had not, but failure to
pay them is for money and so not contempt. More ongoing breaches of the injunction were sworn
to, but there had been no motion for ﬁnding contempt by them, and contempt needs proof beyond
a reasonable doubt. So audience and consideration on the merits were allowed here.⁴
See also Part B.4 above.
E. Miscellaneous
Natural justice and the audi alteram partem rule require the court to give counsel the
opportunity to address a proposed sanction.⁵
A judge asked to punish for contempt of court should alert counsel before imposing a sanction
signiﬁcantly exceeding or differing from that sought by the party asking for punishment or
enforcement, and give both counsel the chance to address the new proposed sanction.⁶
To get a stay of contempt sanctions pending appeal, it is not enough to swear that one lacks
funds to pay the sanctions; clear convincing or cogent evidence in support is needed. And an
expensive lifestyle and unexplained disappearance of assets can be evidence pointing the other
way. Harm to reputation from contempt diminishes after contempt is found.⁷
Someone convicted of contempt can purge his or her contempt only by complying with the
orders or duties disobeyed, albeit not complying perfectly.⁸
There was a ﬁnding that certain
payments were not paid for the ﬁne and did not purge contempt.⁹
Very sloppy incomplete acts (in
answering a questionnaire about assets) were not enough to purge contempt.¹⁰
Breach of a court order is not of itself a ground for damages to another party.¹¹
The court can
give damages for breach of an undertaking by a solicitor.¹²
A witness who fails to appear may also
be liable for any resulting damage.¹³
Failure to disclose facts to the court when seeking an order
ex parte might lead to damages as a remedy?¹⁴

On appeal, the appeal court should be slow to substitute different penalties for those imposed
by a King's Bench justice;¹
the discretion encompasses penalty too.²
Rule 10.53 is discretionary
and so reviewed on appeal for palpable and overriding error.³
An appeal was not ground for
release from jail for contempt pending appeal, where there still was a serious ﬂight risk.⁴
The Supreme Court of Canada’s individual judges have power to give bail pending appeal to
the Supreme Court of Canada from contempt, even civil contempt.⁵
Conviction for contempt does not bar a later prosecution under the Criminal Code, e. g. for
harassment (stalking).⁶
As contempt is a wrong to the court and the public,⁷
it is not surprising that assigning oneself
into bankruptcy may well not stop contempt punishment.⁸
A self-proclaimed Sovereign Free-will Man and his documents and notions ran afoul of the
criminal bail régime.⁹

BOOK_B.title: Punishment for civil contempt of Court

commentary.text: Rule 10.53 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.53. 1. New Rule is Essentially the same as the Old Rule In Koerner v. Capital Health Authority, 2011 ABQB 191, 2011 CarswellAlta 456; affirmed 2011 CarswellAlta 2079 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused 2012 CarswellAlta 724 (S.C.C.), Madam Justice Shelley said, at paragraph 46: 46 R. 10.53 of the Rules of Court outlines the penalties available to a court for civil contempt. It is essentially the same as the penalties set out in Rule 704 of the old Rules. … 2. Factors to Consider … any kind of negligence (advertent or inadvertent, by ommission or commission) is less blameworthy than deliberate defiance of a court order. Reliance upon (mistaken) legal advice has been recognized by some cases as a mitigating factor, when sentence is imposed … Furthermore, where the contempt consists of some type of failure to give discovery, a host of cases say that the object of the exercise is to secure the discovery, more than to punish. Severe punishments, such as summary dismissal, or striking out a defence, have been later remitted after belated compliance, in a number of cases. And any kind of attempt to purge the contempt, or to apologize, is relevant. Michel v. Lafrentz (1998), 68 Alta. L.R. (3d) 140 (C.A.), at 146, per Côté J.A. In Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v. Wenzel (2005), 48 Alta. L.R. (4th) 250 (C.A.), Fraser C.J.A., speaking for the panel, set aside a $5000 penalty assessed against a party found to be in contempt by not producing documents which had been ordered to be produced. At p. 252, Her Ladyship said: In terms of the sanction for contempt, we are of the view that the amount ordered is not adequate for its purpose. Requiring those in contempt to pay a part only of thrown-away costs related directly to the contempt does not bring home to the contemnors the seriousness of their actions and their responsibilities for the consequences attributable to that contempt. There is a public policy aspect to this entire issue. Generally, in principle, those who are found in civil contempt ought, at a minimum, to be required to accept responsibility for a substantial portion of the costs directly related to that contempt. It may be that a judge would also consider it appropriate to impose further monetary penalties or other sanctions, whether including striking of pleadings, drawing of adverse inferences, etc. In the context of this case, it is open to the case management judge in assessing the sanctions which should be imposed to take into account a number of considerations including: (1) the role of counsel, including the extent to which the actions of the respondents' counsel might have contributed to the respondents' contempt; (2) the motivation for the destruction/erasure of the computer records while the undertakings to produce them remained extant; (3) the consequences flowing from the destruction of those records and what redress should flow from that, including consideration of whether any adverse inferences should be drawn as a result thereof; (4) the entire context and history of the litigation; (5) the amount of reasonable thrown-away costs properly incurred; (6) the nature of the contempt; and (7) the degree of culpability of the contemnors. The matter was returned to chamber judge for reconsideration of the appropriate penalty. Greckol J. awarded the plaintiffs their thrown-away costs in the amount of $136,146.27 plus GST. She also ordered production of the missing information, in default of which the defendants were fined $75,000. [See: (2006), 399 A.R. 166 (Alta. Q.B.)] In McDonald Estate, Re, 2013 ABQB 602, 3 CarswellAlta 2002, 573 A.R. 1, Justice Mahoney reviewed the factors to be considered when determining the appropriate penalty for contempt. He said at paragraph 28: 28 As Justice Gates stated in his written reasons when dealing with Ms. Gusa's contempt in the related estate matter before him (McDonald Estate, 2012 ABQB 704, 552 AR 308 at para 55) there is a list of factors to be taken into consideration in determining the penalty for contempt such as: (1) whether there was deliberate defiance of a court order or whether there was an inadvertent failure to comply with the court order; (2) the role of legal counsel; (3) where there has been a failure to give discovery, the object of the exercise is more to secure the discovery rather than to punish; (4) attempts to purge contempt or to apologize are relevant; (5) the entire context in the history of the litigation; (6) the amount of reasonable thrown-away costs properly incurred; (7) the nature of the contempt; and (8) the degree of culpability of the contemnor. In Precision Forest Industries Ltd. v. Cox, 2013 ABQB 524, 2013 CarswellAlta 1772, 574 A.R. 34, Mr. Justice Lee set out the following factors to be considered (at paragraphs 55-56): 55 In addition to the nature of the contemptuous conduct, in determining the appropriate remedy in response to a finding of contempt for breach of a court order, the court may consider factors including: a. whether the contemnor has admitted the breach; b. whether the contemnor has tendered a formal apology to the court; c. whether the breach was a single act of part of an ongoing pattern of conduct; d. whether the breach occurred with the full knowledge and understanding that it was a breach rather than as a result of a mistake or understanding; e. the extent to which the conduct of the contemnor displayed defiance; f. whether the order was a private one, affecting only the parties to the suit of whether come public benefit lay at the root of the order; g. the need for specific and general deterrence; and h. the ability of the contemnor to pay. i. the sanction of contempt should be proportional to the personal responsibility of the person in contempt and to the seriousness of the contempt. 56 In the case of breach of Court Orders which prevents an opposing party from defending an action, it may be appropriate to strike the pleading, but even this should be done on a gradual basis. This type of escalating response is found in for example my decision of S.W. v. K.T., 2005 ABQB 298 where fines and double fines were first imposed because the Plaintiff was unresponsive and contradictory with respect to Answers to the Undertakings, similar to the present case. The Plaintiffs in S.W. were forced to go directly to trial and had to live with their answers. Similarly Kevin Cox is now stuck with his answers to the Questioning until trial, which could prove to be a major problem for him. In Demb v. Valhalla Group Ltd., 2015 ABCA 29, in concurring with the other two Court of Appeal justices in dismissing an appeal from a case management judge's order finding that the defendants were not in contempt, Justice O'Ferrall said that a finding of contempt can have deterrence as its objective. His Lordship said: 38 As the majority correctly points out, the appropriate standard of review demands deference to the case management judge's exercise of discretion. Furthermore, it appears that the case management judge may not yet be finished with respect to the issue of contempt. The order appealed from required the respondents to provide yet another further and better affidavit by September 10, 2013, and two of the respondents failed to file the required affidavit. On the hearing of this appeal, we were advised that a second contempt application had been made to the case management judge. It was adjourned pending this appeal. 39 Although we must defer, I question the respondents' sincerity when it comes to complying with the Rules of Court or with the orders of the Master and the case management judge. The respondents appear to have adopted an attitude of “Let's see how little disclosure we can get away with”. Also, their delays in complying appear to be of their own making. This is not a case where the difficulty in complying with the Rules is disproportionate to the likely benefit. Nor does it appear there are any remaining unresolved issues with respect to the relevancy and materiality of the documents sought. 40 It appears the case management judge adopted the approach that contempt proceedings are designed to compel compliance rather that to punish and fashioned his order with this in mind. While the case management judge was certainly entitled to adopt that approach, there are occasions when it is appropriate to grant contempt orders that have as their object denunciation and deterrence (both specific and general). That is, the sanctions prescribed in Division 4 of Part 10 of the Rules of Court for contravening the Rules and disobeying court orders may be employed to secure compliance; but they also may be employed to denounce and deter such behaviour, communicating to the broader legal community that the court will not accept non-compliance and disobedience as a litigation tactic. 41 Counsel for the appellant quite correctly characterizes repeated and unsanctioned non-compliance with the Rules or orders as a denial of access to justice to the party delayed or denied resolution. I agree. This is a matter the case management judge may yet address in the upcoming contempt proceedings. In Oommen v. Capital Housing Corp., 2016 ABQB 283, 2016 CarswellAlta 903, 87 C.P.C. (7th) 87, Justice Veit adopted the following principles relating to the imposition of sanctions for civil contempt: 37 The recent Crawford decision in Ontario usefully sets out some general principles concerning the sanctioning of civil contempt. Although the decision deals specifically with family law proceedings, the principles apply to all areas of civil litigation. 192 In Cassidy v. Cassidy, 2010 ONSC 2707, [2010] O.J. No. 1927, the Court set out the following regarding sentencing in contempt proceedings: The sanction imposed upon a finding of contempt must be significant and of such consequence as to ensure the administration of justice is not brought into disrepute. Sentencing in contempt proceedings, particular in family law proceedings, should be comprised of two components. It should be restorative to the victim of the contempt and punitive to the contemnor. To accomplish the former requires the sentence to correlate to the conduct that produces the contempt and to accomplish the latter requires the sentence not to reflect a marked departure from those imposed in like circumstances. In determining an appropriate sentence in the present case, considerations include the following: (a) The available sentences: For practical purposes the list of available penalties for civil contempt is a short one, consisting of: no penalty (where the contempt has been purged), a suspended sentence (perhaps conditional upon some act or event occurring), a fine, or incarceration. (b) The proportionality of the sentence to the wrongdoing: A sentence, to be fit, must be proportionate to the gravity of the wrongdoing. Although a finding of contempt carries with it the recognition that the conduct was deliberate and wilful, contempt can reflect degrees of wrongdoing. All instances of contempt are serious, but some are more serious than others. (c) The similarity of sentences in like circumstances: A sentence should not reflect a marked departure from those imposed in like circumstances. Unfortunately, in the area of sentencing for contempt the reported and unreported decisions are scarce. Those that do exist are heavily fact-driven. While each case turns on its own facts, the general principles applied by the court are the same and the penalties differ, depending on the facts. (d) The presence of mitigating factors: An admission of the facts by the contemnor may constitute a mitigating factor. (e) The presence of aggravating factors: That the contemnor's conduct was flagrant and continued over a long period were aggravating factors. (f) Deterrence: The primary purpose of sentencing in contempt proceedings, apart from coercing compliance, is deterrence: both general and specific. The punishment for contempt should serve as a disincentive to those who might be included to breach court orders. (g) The reasonableness of a fine: Where civil contempt is concerned, the ability to pay a fine is a crucial consideration in determining its size. In that case, Lord Romer set out (at p. 418) the general rule that where a person disobeys an order of the court, the court will not entertain any application by that person until he or she obeys the order. He then stated as follows (at p. 420) his reasons for concluding that the general rule should apply: It appears to me that this is the very kind of case in which the ordinary rule should be applied in all its strictness. Disregard of an order of the court is a matter of sufficient gravity, whatever the order may be. Where, however, the order relates to a child the court is (or should be) adamant upon its due observance (cf. the recent case of Corcoran v. Corcoran, [[1950] 1 All E.R. 495]). Such an order is made in the interests of the welfare of the child and the court will not tolerate any interference with or disregard of its decisions upon these matters. The court cannot exercise its quasi-parental powers in relation to a child unless effect can be given to its orders, and it cannot enforce its orders if the child is taken abroad. The matter was put over to March 11, 2005, for decision. The learned justice disagreed with defence counsel, and “held that the Court of Queen's Bench was not without jurisdiction to impose further sanctions with respect to ‘[Braun's] ongoing contempt regarding Orders of this Court.’” Ms. Braun was found to still be in contempt, and was sentenced to another 4-month term of imprisonment (referred to by the Court of Appeal as “sixth Murray order”). The March 11, 2005, order was the subject of this appeal. Berger J.A., speaking for the panel, allowed the accused's appeal, and held that the lower court was functus when it imposed the sentence on March 11, 2005. At pp. 26–27, his Lordship said: The gravamen of the analysis, I suggest, is to ascertain whether (using the criminal law analogy) the impugned act amounts to a new actus reus. A person who is in possession of stolen property over a period of five days is not subject to prosecution for five offences. On the other hand, five bank robberies will attract five charges. The same is true of contempt. Where there is a subsequent breach of a court order stemming from a positive act on the part of the contemnor, such as the breach of a restraining order or a breach of an injunction, the subsequent breach can found a second contempt charge resulting in further sanctions: Skeena Kraft Ltd. v. Pulp & Paper Workers of Canada, supra, and U.N.A. v. Alberta (Attorney General) (1990), 104 A.R. 246 (Alta. C.A.); affirmed [1992] 1 S.C.R. 901 (S.C.C.). On the other hand, if an individual is ordered to attend examinations and wilfully fails to do so, the contempt crystallizes at the moment of non-compliance. Like possession of stolen property, nonattendance the following day does not constitute a new actus reus. If the contempt is not purged, the gravity of disobedience in the context of all of the circumstances is readily ascertained. This includes an assessment of the contemnor's motives for non-compliance, the impact on interested third parties, the public nature of the contempt and its implications for the integrity of the administration of justice. In such circumstances, one way of proceeding would be to adjourn once a finding of contempt is made and to schedule a sentencing hearing at some future date. This would allow the contemnor to consider whether to purge her contempt. If the contemnor elects to purge, that may be a mitigating factor. If the contempt is not purged, continued disobedience is neither an aggravating feature nor a fresh transgression. The sentence imposed should assume continued non-compliance. The nature of the contempt will have been assessed and will have been the subject of judicial pronouncement and sanction. Of course, it is always open to a contemnor to thereafter purge her contempt and to thereby mitigate the punishment that has been imposed. The Court, in my opinion, retains jurisdiction to reduce a fine or a term of imprisonment already imposed when a contemnor later elects to comply with the Court's order. The Court is not functus. Rule 704(4) and the common law preserve the Court's ability, in appropriate circumstances, to vary or remit the sanction. By proceeding in this fashion, respect for the administration of justice is enhanced, certainty is restored, and compliance with court orders is encouraged. Of course, the present restrained and measured practices of the Courts will continue. Judges who find a party to an action in civil contempt will almost always first consider non-penal sanctions such as the striking of pleadings and the imposition of costs. That said, if a penal sanction such as imprisonment or a fine is imposed, the judicial arsenal is not thereby depleted. The Court retains control over its own process and, if the unpurged contempt affects the fair adjudication of the suit, non-penal sanctions may still be invoked. Conclusion For the reasons set out above, I am of the view that the determinate sentence of imprisonment imposed upon the Appellant on October 20, 2004, brought the contempt proceedings to an end. The appeal from the “sixth Murray order” is allowed and that order is vacated. 14. Purging contempt In Lymer (Re), 2020 ABQB 157, 2020 CarswellAlta 398, 11 Alta. L.R. (7th) 157 (Registrar in Bankruptcy), the Registrar (L.A. Smart), gave this guidance as to when a person purges his or her contempt: A. — Purging Contempt (i)—The Test [29] A court may set aside a contempt order where “the contemnor subsequently complies with the order or otherwise purges his or her contempt”: Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, [2015] 2 SCR 79 at para 66 [Carey]. Rule 10.53(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 provides that the Court may waive or suspend penalty or sanction “[i]f a person declared to be in civil contempt of Court purges the person's contempt.” [30] It is the party seeking to purge their contempt who bears the onus of demonstrating on a balance of probabilities that they have done so: Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at paras 23, 29; Korea Data Systems Co v Chiang, 2009 ONCA 3 at paras 50–52 [Chiang]. The contemnor must satisfy the Court that they have subsequently complied with the order they previously breached to the full extent that they are reasonably able: Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at paras 24, 29; Lymer (Re), 2018 ABQB 859 at para 157; Turkawski v 738675 Alberta Ltd, 2007 ABQB 745 at para 37 [Turkawski I]. (ii)—Principles [31] The objectives and principles that govern the contempt power are relevant to determining whether a party held in contempt has subsequently purged that contempt. [32] It is vital for a court to be able to enforce compliance with its orders: “The rule of law is directly dependent on the ability of the courts to enforce their process and maintain their dignity and respect” (Carey at para 30, citing United Nurses of Alberta v Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 SCR 901 at 931, 1992 CanLII 99). A civil contempt order has as its main purpose coercion—to promote compliance with a court's orders (Chiang at para 117; Demb v Valhalla Group Ltd, 2017 ABQB 256 at paras 54, 82 [Demb ABQB 2017], aff'd 2017 ABCA 340 [Demb ABCA 2017], citing Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42 at para 59). This power, however, is one that courts must use “cautiously and with great restraint” (Carey at para 36, citing TG Industries Ltd v Williams, 2001 NSCA 105 at para 32). As such, a judge may decline to make a finding in contempt where the alleged contemnor acted in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply with a court order (Carey at para 37). [33] However, it is also important to recognize that, as stated by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Knapp v Munro, 2015 ONSC 5444 at para 16: Notwithstanding the court's reluctance to exercise it contempt powers, it is important that such powers be exercised in appropriate cases to ensure that parties … understand that court orders cannot be ignored or disobeyed, and that compliance with a court order is neither an option nor a bargaining chip. [34] A court assessing whether a party has purged their contempt should also consider the context of the original contempt order and the circumstances of the overarching litigation (see e.g. Turkawski I; Turkawski v 738675 Alberta Ltd, 2008 ABQB 27 at paras 4-5, 15 [Turkawski II]; Keephills Aggregate Co v Riverview Properties Inc., 2008 ABQB 540 at para 18 [Keephills]; Demb ABCA 2017 at paras 5-6). … [37] It may be possible for a party found in contempt to purge their contempt without achieving perfect compliance with the order they previously breached. This may be the case where the party shows that they are unable—as opposed to unwilling—to satisfy elements of the earlier order (Turkawski I at para 37; Turkawski II at para 15). Additionally, the court may take into consideration that “the passage of time, and other factors, may affect the true importance of receiving complete satisfaction” of an earlier undertaking or requirement (Turkawski I at para 32). The fact that a party has not achieved perfect compliance with an earlier requirement may be less important where the intended product of that requirement is no longer relevant (Turkawski I at para 53). [38] Similarly, when document production is at the heart of the earlier contempt finding, a court may consider whether production has “run its course” at the time that a party applies to purge its contempt (Demb ABCA 2017 at para 6). … [45] The party seeking to purge its contempt holds the burden of showing that they have complied with the court order they previously breached or that despite their reasonable efforts, they are unable to do so: Turkawski I at para 37; Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at paras 24, 29. It is not enough to show merely that any outstanding obligations are extremely difficult or onerous: Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at para 27. However, context is an important consideration: see e.g. Turkawski I; Turkawski II at paras 4–5 15; Kee hills at para 18; Demb ABCA 2017 at paras 5–6
